A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and are readable throughout, including their equations, figures, tables and references. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix or the separately referenced supplementary material.

before.justification: v1 reports original planner evaluations and numerical interaction-synthesis results on FullBodyManipulation and random long trajectories (Tables 1–2).

after.justification: v2 reports original interaction-synthesis results, human preference studies and physics-tracking experiments (Table 1, Figures 4 and 6, Section 7.3).

M1.justification: v2 adds a PPO-based physics tracker with importance sampling after kinematic motion generation (Section 6). Contact-phase segmentation changes from object velocity to predicted contact labels separately for each hand, and RefineNet gains an explicitly specified wrist-object relative-pose loss.

E1.justification: FullBodyManipulation, GRAB, HumanML3D and everyday scene-rearrangement coverage remain. v2 substantially extends the evaluated tasks to reference-motion tracking and object manipulation under physical simulation, introducing dynamics-constrained execution beyond v1's kinematic evaluations.

E2.justification: Alongside the retained CNet/CHOIS and C+RNet comparisons, v2 evaluates CHOIS combined with GRIP in Table 1 and PhysHOI against the physics tracker in Section 7.3/Figure 8. GRIP was cited in v1 but was not an evaluated comparator there.

E3.justification: Planner evaluation specifies GPT-4o instead of GPT-4V. Interaction evaluation retains waypoint error but replaces the other original metrics with broader foot-motion, contact, intersection-volume and ground-truth-error measures. New perception studies use 20 AMT raters per pair; the motion study specifies 15 sequences per method and 60 pairs. Physics tracking introduces reference-motion error evaluation.

E4.justification: The CNet and C+RNet ablations remain, with new human preference evidence about their perceptual effects. v2 adds kinematic-versus-physics artifact cases and a PhysHOI grasp-failure comparison (Figures 7–8). v1's separate quantitative long-trajectory stress analysis in Table 2 is absent, although its qualitative examples are reused in v2 Figure 5.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental seeds, independent-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's rater counts describe study sample sizes, without introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 contains revised values and many new result entries: the full model's reported waypoint error changes from 2.01 to 2.81 cm. v2 additionally reports 71.9% planner preference, approximately 2 cm tracking error and a foot-sliding score of 0.002; v1's long-trajectory table is absent. The PDFs do not establish identical settings for controlled cross-version performance comparisons.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.2.3 adds coordinate transformations and a contact-masked surface-point loss defining wrist-object relative-pose consistency (Equations 2–4). v1 describes relative-pose conditioning without this mathematical formulation. The existing diffusion formulation remains, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The retained contribution of instruction-driven synchronized human, object and finger motion expands to include physically simulated execution. v2 makes physics tracking central to the abstract, introduction and conclusion, and newly claims superiority supported by quantitative, qualitative and human-study comparisons.

C2.justification: v2 attributes preference over fingerless motion-capture data to its synthesized finger details and interprets physics tracking as correcting kinematic artifacts. Its conclusion adds discussion of scene representations, planning in complex environments and grasp-success limitations, absent from v1's conclusion.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents 20,000 grasp-surface samples, 100 object points for the relative-pose loss, wrist post-processing and standard split references. The grasp sample-count comparison is against DexGraspNet, not a stated v1 budget. Conversely, v1's graph cycle handling, BPS sampling constants and left-hand mirroring details are omitted; this establishes disclosure changes, not removal of those procedures.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial Physics-Based Motion Synthesis discussion, positioning the system relative to DeepMimic, AMP, OmniGrasp and PhysHOI. These additions establish a new research connection to simulated motion imitation, alongside expanded references on scene generation and language-based motion planning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method descriptions undergo extensive condensation and rewriting. Spatial-relationship generation and layout calculation become Scene Map Generation, diffusion background receives a separate subsection, and experiments are reorganized by module. Terminology changes from task plans to execution plans, and the author list adds Pei Xu.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to double-column layout, with redrawn pipeline diagrams and an expanded first-page teaser. Table 1 grows from three methods and five metrics to four methods and eleven metrics; the long-trajectory table disappears. Earlier qualitative panels are reused within expanded comparisons, and preference charts and physics-comparison figures are added.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluates detailed-finger realism mainly through component ablations. v2 adds CHOIS+GRIP, targeted hand-interaction metrics and human preference evidence, including 68% preference over CHOIS+GRIP, substantially strengthening support for the central contribution. Physics-tracking experiments also support the expanded execution claim. Losing dedicated long-trajectory scores and leaving tracker training details outside the supplied PDF limit verification, but the stronger comparative validation provides a substantial overall quality improvement.
